🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.38% (intraday, 7-year +5bp). At trading day 43 (last close) it was -0.51% against a five-campaign average of -1.63% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.77%. The 10-year is +9bp since the hike vs a +18bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 772bp against a five-year average of 421bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is holding: single-B -2bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.34 → 0.64 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+4bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,108bp, +1bp since 2026-11-13, 87bp under the Oct 15 record and 656bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 81.1 (14.6%, -0.6pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 132bp, Oracle 304bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -24%, NBIS -38%, IREN -40% vs NVDA -25%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 28 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -16.7% vs -16.5% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 34% in 3m, 31% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 50%. 6m odds -6.1pp since 2026-11-12. Triggered signposts: Basket names >20% off high; SOX.
  • Stocks: US stocks fell hard, led by tech, ahead of Nvidia's results tomorrow.

Monday was a broad de-risking session led by technology. The S&P 500 fell 1.918624% to 7416.59 (-145.08), the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.492454% to 24509.76, the Dow fell 1.412444% to 51608.17 and the Russell 2000 fell 1.703966% to 2742.941. The VIX jumped 18.70466% to 22.91 from 19.3. The selloff started in Asia (Nikkei -2.421121%) and stayed contained in Europe (Euro Stoxx 50 -0.6029567%, STOXX 600 -0.2755443%, FTSE 100 -0.192707%). Within the S&P, Info Tech fell -2.98% and Comm Services -2.82%, while Staples (+0.34%) and Utilities (+0.12%) rose: a defensive rotation, not a liquidation. Oil also fell (Brent -4.267529215358935% to 91.75), and Treasuries were mixed (2Y -1.25bp to 4.8294, 30Y +0.86bp to 5.4741). The phase model's signposts matter today. Two have now triggered: breadth (57.14% of the tech basket is more than 20% off its high, against a 50% line) and the SOX (-30.67% from its 52-week high, past the -30% line). Even so, the model still puts the basket in Phase 1, 'initial drop, credit calm', on day 28 since the peak. The 6-month Phase-2/3 odds fell 6.1pp versus the 2026-11-12 run, and the defensive step stays at 1 - Cautious (since 2026-11-05). HY contagion: the Caa-B gap is 772bp. That is the 98.98 percentile of its 5-year history, versus a 5-year average of 420.5bp, after widening +194bp over 3 months and +48bp over 1 month, and the dataset flags it as widest since 2020-04-16. The FRED CCC-B cross-check agrees (975bp, 98.98 percentile). The stress has not yet spread up the quality ladder. Single-B OAS is 311bp (+1bp in 1 month), Ba is 182bp (-12bp in 1 month), the B-Ba gap of 129bp is in line with its 128.8bp 5-year average, and IG is 86bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.64 from 0.35 three months ago, but it is still below its 0.69 5-year median. This is a descriptive reading, not a signal. On AI credit, CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1107.9bp, still 86.6bp below the 1,194.5bp record and 162bp tighter on the week, and Nvidia CDS was unchanged at 131.84bp. The credit market is not pricing a backstop failure into Nvidia's results tomorrow. Sentiment: fearful in equities, complacent in credit.

“Tech is bleeding and CCCs are burning, but until BB and IG spreads move, this is a correction with a fever, not a credit crisis.”
📊Markets

US equities had their worst day in some time. The S&P 500 closed at 7416.59 (-1.918624%, -145.08), the Nasdaq Composite at 24509.76 (-2.492454%, -626.51), the Dow at 51608.17 (-1.412444%, -739.38) and the Russell 2000 at 2742.941 (-1.703966%). The Nasdaq underperformed the Dow by more than 1pp, so this was a growth/AI unwind rather than a macro shock. The VIX rose 3.61 points to 22.91. Japan led the global decline (Nikkei 59662.02, -2.421121%), and Europe fell less than half as much as the US. In rates, the US 2Y fell 1.25bp to 4.8294, the 10Y slipped 0.41bp to 5.1311 and the 30Y rose 0.86bp to 5.4741, a mild steepening. Abroad, Gilts rose +3bp to 5.365, Bunds +1.2bp to 3.389 and JGBs +2.1bp to 2.892. The global long end is not rallying even on a risk-off day, which limits duration as a hedge. Commodities fell: WTI 85.72 (-3.206865401987357%), Brent 91.75 (-4.267529215358935%), copper -1.3627780970363608%, nat gas -3.3436532507739964%. Gold was flat at 3856.04.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.49 vol points (17th percentile of the 70 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.3 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 89bp (flatter by 2bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (103bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 47 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 62/100 — Underlying inflation is sticky but not re-accelerating broadly. Core PCE YoY is 3.12115 and core sticky CPI is 3.0595, both above the trimmed and median gauges (Median CPI 2.8, 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.9, Median PCE 2.66557, trimmed-mean PCE 2.26). The computed core-trend sub-score sits modestly above its historical middle, and four of its five inputs are rising or flat. Breadth is split: 26.8% of the PCE basket is rising faster than 5% (16.6% above 10%, 10.2% at 5-10%), but 25.6% is outright falling. Flexible CPI at 6.201 shows the pressure is in volatile components (energy), and today's 4% Brent drop eases that. Market expectations are anchored: 1y breakeven 1.9662, 5y 2.257. Wages are not driving it (AHE 3.1, ECI 0.8). Net: persistence is moderate. That is enough to keep a hawkish Fed on track for December, not enough to justify a series of hikes.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy is about how a bust unfolds, not about valuation. The 2000 bust took the Nasdaq down 78% over 31 months from 2000-03-10, and its first leg was likewise an equity drop with calm credit. Today's starting valuation is much lower (the Nasdaq P/E is a fraction of the 2000 peak), so the downside if the analogy holds should be smaller. The vulnerability is elsewhere: very loose financial conditions, tight IG/Baa spreads, crowded positioning and concentration (my estimate is about 38% top-10 weight; CAPE about 37x; market cap to GDP about 205%, all analyst estimates not verified this run). The AI neocloud credit complex (CoreWeave CDS 1107.9bp, NBIS/IREN drawdowns of -59.6%/-73.2%) is the pressure point. CCC stress at the 98.98 percentile shows the weakest borrowers are already repricing. What would move this from Phase 1 to Phase 2 is credit confirmation: HY OAS through 420-448bp, Baa-10Y through 195bp, or CoreWeave CDS through its 1,194.5bp record. Nvidia's results on 2026-11-17 are the near-term catalyst for all three.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

A 25bp hike at the December 8-9 FOMC is the base case. After the October hold at 3.75%-4.00%, markets had priced about 88% odds, the move left 'squarely on the table', and two members dissented in favour of an immediate hike. Inference: Warsh has refused to pre-commit, so a hold remains possible if the equity drawdown tightens financial conditions sharply. Today's NFCI (-0.46) still shows loose conditions, which argues against delay.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his on-record framework: a data-dependent, somewhat hawkish path with less forward guidance, fewer meetings (a planned move to a 'six plus two' schedule over two years) and continued attention to balance-sheet size. Given core PCE at 3.12115 and unemployment at 4.1, one to two further hikes over 12 months is plausible. That is an analyst estimate, not a market price.

Warsh's stated approach is to avoid prejudging meetings; he named the October and December meetings as decision points for output, jobs and inflation. The Fed upgraded growth from 'solid' to 'strong' in October. PIMCO characterises a Warsh Fed as a 'thoughtful policy approach' rather than a reflexively dovish one. Flag: the 12-month view is my inference from these statements; no source gives a forecast path.
